en: be based on; be grounded in

examples.en: This decision was made based on the law.
Please speak based on the facts.
That article was based on solid data.
A judgment grounded in principle is needed.

examples.ko: 우리 회사는 고객 중심 원칙에 입각해 일할 거예요.
examples.en: Our company will work based on a customer-first principle.

examples.ko: 경험에 입각하지 않은 조언은 도움이 안 돼요.
examples.en: Advice that is not based on experience does not help.

explain: 거의 항상 '~에 입각해(서)'의 꼴로 써요. 앞에는 법, 사실, 원칙, 자료처럼 근거가 되는 말이 와요. 말할 때보다 뉴스나 글에서 더 자주 보이고, 일상에서는 '~에 따라서', '~을 바탕으로'가 더 편해요.
explain_en: It almost always appears in the pattern '~에 입각해(서)'. What comes before it is a source of grounds, such as law, fact, principle, or data. You see it more in news and writing than in speech; in daily talk '~에 따라서' or '~을 바탕으로' feels easier.

examples.en: The Earth rotates once a day.
Venus rotated very slowly.
The direction in which planets rotate differs from one to another.
The Moon also rotates and goes around the Earth.
Day and night happen because the Earth rotates.
How fast does Saturn rotate?

explain: 자기 둘레를 도는 건 '자전', 다른 별 둘레를 도는 건 '공전'이에요. 지구는 자전하면서 동시에 태양 둘레를 공전해요. 일상 대화에는 거의 안 나오고 과학 수업이나 뉴스에서 써요.
explain_en: Turning around its own axis is 자전, and going around another body is 공전. The Earth rotates and, at the same time, revolves around the Sun. It hardly shows up in everyday talk; you meet it in science class or the news.

examples.ko: 그 가게는 오십 년째 존속하고 있어요.
examples.en: That shop has continued to exist for fifty years.
This system will continue to exist in the future too.
For the company to survive, new investment is needed.
That organization survived even during the war.

examples.ko: 오래 존속해 온 전통을 지키고 싶어요.
examples.en: I want to protect a tradition that has lasted a long time.
It is hard for the theater to survive this way.

explain: 비슷한 '유지하다'는 사람이 애써서 지킬 때 쓰고, '존속하다'는 회사·제도·단체가 사라지지 않고 이어질 때 써요. 주어가 사람이 아닌 경우가 대부분이에요. 뉴스나 글에서 많이 보여요.
explain_en: '유지하다' is for something a person works to keep going, while '존속하다' is for a company, system, or group that does not disappear and carries on. The subject is almost never a person. You see it often in news and writing.

en: aspire to; apply for (a career, school, or major)

examples.en: There are many students in the classroom who aspire to be writers.
My younger sibling is aiming to become a nurse.
He aspired to be an actor from childhood.
I'm happy I got into the department I applied for.
Which department are you going to apply to?
I came up to Seoul because I aspire to be a singer.

explain: 되고 싶은 직업이나 가고 싶은 학교·학과를 목표로 삼을 때 써요. 서류를 내는 '지원하다'보다 마음속 목표에 가까워요. '작가 지망생'처럼 명사 '지망생'으로도 자주 들려요.
explain_en: Use it when you set a job you want or a school or major you want to enter as your goal. It sits closer to a goal in your mind than '지원하다', which is handing in an application. The noun '지망생', as in '작가 지망생', is also very common.

examples.en: Many religions believe in a creator.

examples.ko: 창조주가 세상을 만들었다고 생각하는 사람들이 있어요.
examples.en: Some people think a creator made the world.

examples.ko: 그 화가는 자신을 작은 창조주라고 불렀어요.
examples.en: That painter called himself a little creator.
They offered a prayer of thanks to the Creator.

examples.ko: 이 영화는 창조주와 인간의 관계를 다뤄요.
examples.en: This film deals with the relationship between the Creator and humans.
I said I wanted to know the Creator's will.

explain: 주로 종교 이야기에서 세상을 만든 존재를 가리킬 때 써요. 기독교에서는 보통 '하나님'이라고 부르고, '창조주'는 만든 분이라는 역할을 말하고 싶을 때 써요. 새로운 것을 만든 사람에게 비유로 붙이기도 해요.
explain_en: It is used mostly in religious talk for the being who made the world. In Christianity people usually say '하나님'; '창조주' is chosen when the speaker wants to stress the role of maker. It can also be used figuratively for someone who made something new.

examples.en: A creditor came to the company today.
We have to pay the creditors back.
The bank is the biggest creditor.
I met with the creditor and talked about how to pay it back.
A meeting of creditors will be held next week.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 채권자를 피해 이사를 갔어요.
examples.en: That person moved away to avoid the creditors.

explain: 돈을 받을 사람이 채권자이고, 갚아야 할 사람은 '채무자'예요. 두 말은 짝이라서 같이 외우면 좋아요. 은행·회사·뉴스 이야기에서 자주 나와요. 개인끼리일 때는 보통 '돈을 빌려준 사람'이라고 말해요.
explain_en: The person who is owed money is the 채권자, and the person who has to pay is the '채무자'. They are a pair, so it helps to learn them together. It often appears in talk about banks, companies, and the news. Between individuals people usually say '돈을 빌려준 사람'.

examples.ko: 작은 말다툼이 큰 싸움의 촉발이 됐어요.
examples.en: A small argument became the trigger for a big fight.
That incident was what set off the protest.
They are investigating the cause that set it off.
This announcement led to a controversy being set off.
Finding the triggering factor is important.
When was the point at which the economic crisis was set off?

explain: '~의 촉발', '촉발 원인'처럼 다른 말 앞뒤에 붙여 써요. 혼자 쓰기보다 동사 '촉발하다', '촉발되다'가 더 흔해요. 일상에서는 '계기'를 많이 쓰고, '촉발'은 뉴스·보고서 같은 딱딱한 글에서 써요.
explain_en: It is attached to other words, as in '~의 촉발' or '촉발 원인'. The verbs '촉발하다' and '촉발되다' are more common than the noun alone. In daily talk people say '계기'; '촉발' belongs to stiff writing such as news and reports.

examples.en: The conflict was triggered by a small misunderstanding.

examples.ko: 그 발언으로 논란이 촉발될 수 있어요.
examples.en: That remark could set off a controversy.
This protest was set off by the ruling.
A single mistake can set off a war.
My anxiety was set off and I couldn't sleep.
It is a situation in which emotions are easily set off.

explain: 일이 저절로 터져 나오는 느낌이에요. 주어는 갈등, 논란, 시위, 감정처럼 '벌어지는 일'이 와요. 누가 일으켰는지 말하고 싶으면 '촉발하다'를 써요. 사람이 주어로 오지는 않아요.
explain_en: It feels like something bursting out on its own. The subject is an event that breaks out, such as a conflict, controversy, protest, or emotion. When you want to say who caused it, use '촉발하다'. A person does not serve as the subject.

examples.en: That remark set off a big controversy.

examples.ko: 작은 사고가 대형 사고를 촉발할 수 있어요.
examples.en: A small accident can set off a major accident.
A price hike triggers protests from consumers.
I want to avoid sounds that trigger anxiety.
The new policy ended up setting off protests.
What was it that set off this conflict?

explain: '갈등, 논란, 분쟁, 시위' 같은 말과 자주 붙어요. 비슷한 '일으키다'는 일상 대화에서도 쓰고, '촉발하다'는 어떤 일이 터지는 계기가 됐을 때 뉴스나 글에서 써요. 반대로 일이 터지는 쪽에서 말하면 '촉발되다'예요.
explain_en: It often pairs with words like conflict, controversy, dispute, and protest. The similar '일으키다' also works in daily talk, while '촉발하다' fits news and writing when something became the spark. Seen from the side of the thing that breaks out, it becomes '촉발되다'.

en: be exhibited; be entered (in a contest or show)

examples.en: That film was entered in a film festival.
My photo will be entered in the contest.

examples.ko: 올해 박람회에는 새 제품이 많이 출품돼요.
examples.en: Many new products are exhibited at this year's expo.
I went and saw all of the submitted works.
That novel could not be entered for the literary prize.
I'm glad my work was entered in the exhibition.

explain: '출품하다'는 내놓는 쪽, '출품되다'는 내놓아지는 쪽 이야기예요. 영화제·공모전·전시회·박람회 앞에 '~에'를 붙여요. 주어는 사진, 영화, 그림 같은 작품이에요. 학교 대회에 낼 때는 보통 '내다', '제출하다'라고 해요.
explain_en: '출품하다' is told from the side that puts a work forward, and '출품되다' from the side of the work being put forward. Add '~에' after a film festival, contest, exhibition, or expo. The subject is a work such as a photo, film, or painting. For a school competition people usually say '내다' or '제출하다'.

en: exhibit; enter (a work) in a contest or show; submit

examples.en: I entered a painting in this contest.

examples.ko: 감독은 영화를 해외 영화제에 출품할 계획이에요.
examples.en: The director plans to enter the film in an overseas film festival.
Companies show their new products at the expo.
It is the day students submit their works.
After entering my photo, I wait for the result.

examples.ko: 어떤 작품을 출품할지 아직 못 정했어요.
examples.en: I haven't decided yet which work to enter.

explain: 영화제, 공모전, 전시회, 박람회에 작품이나 제품을 내놓을 때 써요. 목적어는 작품이고 장소 앞에는 '~에'를 붙여요. 그냥 서류를 내는 건 '제출하다'이고, 작품을 대회나 전시에 올릴 때가 '출품하다'예요.
explain_en: Use it when putting a work or product forward to a film festival, contest, exhibition, or expo. The object is the work, and the venue takes '~에'. Handing in plain paperwork is '제출하다'; putting a work into a contest or show is '출품하다'.

examples.en: My uncle works at a civil engineering company.
I majored in civil engineering at university.

examples.ko: 이 다리는 토목 기술이 좋아서 튼튼해요.
examples.en: This bridge is sturdy because of good civil engineering.
The road is blocked because of construction work.
I'm preparing for the civil engineer exam.
He has worked in the civil engineering field for a long time.

explain: 건축은 건물을 짓는 일이고, 토목은 도로·다리·댐·터널처럼 모두가 쓰는 시설을 만드는 일이에요. '토목 공사', '토목 공학'처럼 다른 명사 앞에 붙여 써요. 한자로는 흙(土)과 나무(木)지만 그 뜻으로 쓰지는 않아요.
explain_en: 건축 is building construction, while 토목 is making facilities everyone uses, such as roads, bridges, dams, and tunnels. It is attached before other nouns, as in '토목 공사' and '토목 공학'. The characters mean soil (土) and wood (木), but the word is not used in that literal sense.

examples.ko: 도박은 한 사람의 삶을 파멸시킬 수 있어요.
examples.en: Gambling can ruin a person's life.
His lies brought the company down.
War destroys cities.
Be careful that greed doesn't ruin your family.

examples.ko: 그 소문이 그녀의 인생을 파멸시키고 말았어요.
examples.en: That rumor ended up ruining her life.

examples.ko: 한 번의 선택이 나라를 파멸시킨 적이 있어요.
examples.en: A single choice has ruined a country before.

explain: '파멸하다'는 스스로 무너지는 일이고, '파멸시키다'는 누가 또는 무엇이 다른 것을 무너뜨리는 일이에요. 목적어로 삶, 인생, 가족, 회사처럼 큰 것이 와요. 일상 대화보다 이야기와 뉴스에 나오는 센 표현이에요.
explain_en: '파멸하다' is falling apart by oneself, and '파멸시키다' is someone or something bringing another thing down. The object is something big, like a life, family, or company. It is a strong expression found in stories and the news more than in daily talk.

en: be ruined; go to ruin; collapse

examples.en: If you give in to greed, you end up ruined.
That company was ruined by debt.

examples.ko: 도박에 빠진 사람은 파멸할 수 있어요.
examples.en: A person who falls into gambling can be ruined.

examples.ko: 이대로 가면 우리 모두 파멸하고 말 거예요.
examples.en: If we go on like this, we will all end up ruined.

examples.ko: 그는 파멸하는 길인 줄 알면서도 멈추지 못했어요.
examples.en: He knew it was a path to ruin but could not stop.
They rebuilt the country that had gone to ruin.

explain: 돈, 건강, 관계, 나라처럼 큰 것이 완전히 무너져 다시 일어나기 힘들 때 써요. '실패하다'보다 훨씬 무겁고 되돌릴 수 없다는 느낌이 있어요. 주어는 사람, 회사, 나라가 올 수 있어요.
explain_en: Use it when something big, such as money, health, a relationship, or a country, collapses so completely that recovery is hard. It is much heavier than '실패하다' and carries a feeling that it cannot be undone. The subject can be a person, company, or country.

en: breakdown; collapse (of a marriage, finances, or relationship)

examples.ko: 그 부부는 결혼 생활이 파탄에 이르렀어요.
examples.en: That couple's marriage reached a breakdown.
The company's finances are on the verge of collapse.
I try not to let the relationship fall apart.
The country's economy was in a state of collapse.
The family fell apart because of debt.
To prevent a collapse, we have to cut spending.

explain: '파탄 나다', '파탄에 이르다', '파탄을 맞다'처럼 써요. 재정, 결혼, 관계, 경제처럼 이어 가야 하는 것이 더는 이어지지 않을 때 쓰는 말이에요. 일 하나가 안 된 '실패'와 달리 전체가 무너졌다는 느낌이에요.
explain_en: It appears in set phrases like '파탄 나다', '파탄에 이르다', and '파탄을 맞다'. It is for things that have to keep going, such as finances, marriage, relationships, or an economy, when they can no longer continue. Unlike '실패', one failed task, it feels like the whole thing has fallen apart.

examples.en: We measured the salt content of the seawater.

examples.ko: 해수는 짜서 그냥 마실 수 없어요.
examples.en: Seawater is salty, so you can't just drink it.
The seawater around the beach is clear.
This plant turns seawater into fresh water.
The typhoon grew stronger because the seawater temperature was high.
Seawater contains a lot of salt.

explain: 일상에서는 '바닷물'이라고 하고, '해수'는 과학이나 뉴스에서 써요. 반대로 강이나 호수의 물은 '담수'나 '민물'이라고 해요. '해수욕'에도 이 글자가 들어 있어요.
explain_en: In daily life people say '바닷물'; '해수' is for science and the news. Water from rivers and lakes is '담수' or '민물'. The same characters appear in '해수욕', swimming at the sea.

examples.en: He is called the very embodiment of honesty.
She seems the very picture of kindness.

examples.ko: 이 소설 속 악당은 탐욕의 화신이에요.
examples.en: The villain in this novel is the embodiment of greed.

examples.ko: 마을 사람들은 그 아이를 희망의 화신으로 여겼어요.
examples.en: The villagers regarded that child as the embodiment of hope.

examples.ko: 검소함의 화신인 할머니는 물건을 안 버려요.
examples.en: My grandmother, the embodiment of thrift, never throws things away.

examples.ko: 사랑의 화신이 된 것처럼 모두에게 잘해 줬어요.
examples.en: As if she had become love itself, she was kind to everyone.

explain: 거의 항상 'X의 화신' 꼴로 써요. X에는 정직, 탐욕, 사랑, 악처럼 성질을 나타내는 말이 와요. 칭찬에도 비난에도 쓰고, 그 성질이 사람 모습으로 나타난 것 같다는 강한 비유예요.
explain_en: It almost always appears in the form 'X의 화신'. X is a quality such as honesty, greed, love, or evil. It can praise or criticize, and it is a strong figure of speech saying that quality seems to have taken human form.

examples.en: The company decided to cut staff this year.
The government cut the budget.
Efforts to reduce carbon emissions are needed.
Even if we cut costs, we have to keep up quality.
We had no choice but to cut production.
Discussions continue over the issue of cutting troops.

explain: '줄이다'는 일상에서 뭐든 줄일 때 쓰고, '감축하다'는 인원, 예산, 배출량, 생산량처럼 수나 양을 정책이나 계획으로 줄일 때 써요. 반대말은 '증원하다', '늘리다'예요. 뉴스와 회사 글에서 자주 보여요.
explain_en: '줄이다' works for reducing anything in daily life, while '감축하다' is for cutting numbers or amounts by policy or plan, such as staff, budget, emissions, or output. Opposites are '증원하다' and '늘리다'. You often see it in the news and in company documents.

en: miss a game; sit out (due to injury, etc.)

examples.en: The captain will sit out the next game due to injury.

examples.ko: 그 선수는 두 달 동안 결장했어요.
examples.en: That player was out for two months.

examples.ko: 에이스가 결장할 때 팀 성적이 떨어졌어요.
examples.en: The team's results dropped when the ace was out.
Many players are missing games because of colds.
He came back to the stadium for the first time after being out.

examples.ko: 그가 결장한 경기에서 우리 팀이 이겼어요.
examples.en: Our team won the game he missed.

explain: 스포츠 뉴스에서 선수가 부상이나 징계로 경기에 나오지 못할 때 써요. 반대말은 '출전하다'예요. 학교나 모임에 안 나오는 건 '결석하다', '불참하다'라고 하고 '결장하다'는 쓰지 않아요.
explain_en: In sports news it is for a player who cannot play because of injury or suspension. The opposite is '출전하다'. Not showing up at school or a meeting is '결석하다' or '불참하다'; '결장하다' is not used for that.

en: communicate (by radio or signal); exchange messages

examples.en: The pilot communicates with the control tower.
The astronaut communicated with Earth every day.
I was worried because we couldn't make contact with the ship.
In the mountains, some people communicate by walkie-talkie.
After communicating with the rescue team, we learned the location.

examples.ko: 우리는 짧게 교신한 뒤에 연락이 끊겼어요.
examples.en: We were in contact briefly, and then the connection was lost.

explain: 무전기, 신호, 통신 장비로 주고받을 때 써요. 비행기, 배, 우주, 구조 상황에서 자주 나와요. 일상에서 전화나 문자로 소식을 주고받는 건 '연락하다'라고 해요.
explain_en: It is for exchanging messages through radios, signals, or communication equipment. It comes up often with planes, ships, space, and rescue situations. Trading news by phone or text in daily life is '연락하다'.

examples.en: Our factory supplies parts to a large company.
We have to deliver the products by tomorrow.

examples.ko: 그 회사는 학교에 급식 재료를 납품했어요.
examples.en: That company supplied food ingredients to the school.
We loaded the goods to be delivered onto the truck.

examples.ko: 싼 가격에 납품하는 업체를 찾고 있어요.
examples.en: I'm looking for a company that supplies at a low price.

examples.ko: 납품하고 나면 대금을 받을 수 있어요.
examples.en: Once we deliver, we can get paid.

explain: 주문한 회사나 기관에 물건을 가져다줄 때 써요. 회사끼리의 거래라서 개인에게 보내는 '배송하다', '배달하다'와 달라요. 돈은 보통 납품한 뒤에 받아요. 받는 쪽에서는 '납품받다'라고 해요.
explain_en: Use it when bringing goods to the company or organization that ordered them. It is a business-to-business matter, so it differs from '배송하다' or '배달하다', which go to individuals. Payment usually comes after delivery. From the receiving side it is '납품받다'.

en: be unofficially decided; be tipped (for a post)

examples.en: He has been unofficially picked as the next president.

examples.ko: 신입 사원 한 명이 해외 지사로 내정돼요.
examples.en: One new employee is being lined up for an overseas branch.
There is a rumor that a candidate has already been chosen.
An article came out saying he had been lined up as the director.
People say he will be tipped for minister.
It hasn't been decided yet, so please wait.

explain: 공식 발표 전에 속으로 먼저 정해졌을 때 써요. 사장, 감독, 장관, 후보 같은 직책이나 인사 이야기에 나와요. 발표까지 끝나서 확실해진 건 '확정되다'라고 해요.
explain_en: Use it when something has been settled behind the scenes before the official announcement. It appears with posts and personnel, such as a president, coach, minister, or candidate. Once it is announced and certain, the word is '확정되다'.

en: decide unofficially in advance; line up (someone for a post)

examples.en: The chairman has already lined up his successor.
I heard the company has lined up a new CEO.

examples.ko: 아직 발표 전이지만 팀장을 내정해 두었어요.
examples.en: It's before the announcement, but we've already picked the team leader.
Who are you thinking of lining up for that post?

examples.ko: 미리 내정하는 방식은 불공평하다는 말이 있어요.
examples.en: Some say that picking people in advance is unfair.
After settling on the coach, we moved on to the contract.

explain: 공식 발표나 절차 전에 사람을 마음속으로 정해 둘 때 써요. '정하다'와 달리 아직 밖에 알리지 않았다는 느낌이 있어요. 주로 직책과 인사 이야기에서 써요. 정해진 쪽에서 말하면 '내정되다'예요.
explain_en: Use it when someone is chosen in private before the official announcement or procedure. Unlike '정하다', it carries a feeling that it has not been made public yet. It is mainly used for posts and personnel. From the side of the person chosen, it becomes '내정되다'.

examples.en: Please knock first before you go in.
He knocked quietly on the door.
Even when I knock on the meeting room door, there is no answer.

examples.ko: 사장님 방에 들어갈 때는 노크해야 해요.
examples.en: You have to knock when you enter the boss's office.
I heard the sound of someone knocking on the door.
I knocked and waited, but nobody came out.

explain: '문을 노크하다'처럼 '문을'과 함께 써요. 영어 knock에서 온 말이라 일상에서도 '문을 두드리다'보다 '노크하다'를 더 자주 말해요. '두드리다'는 세게 여러 번 칠 때 써요. 소리를 말할 때는 '노크 소리'라고 해요.
explain_en: It goes with '문을', as in '문을 노크하다'. It comes from English 'knock', and in daily talk people say '노크하다' more often than '문을 두드리다'. '두드리다' is for hitting hard, several times. For the sound, people say '노크 소리'.

en: stand up to; take on (an opponent)

examples.en: The small team took on the title favorite.
It's hard to take on ten people alone.
There is no player who can match him.

examples.ko: 우리는 강한 상대와 대적해 볼 생각이에요.
examples.en: We plan to try going up against a strong opponent.

examples.ko: 대적하는 두 나라의 관계가 점점 나빠졌어요.
examples.en: The relationship between the two opposing countries got worse and worse.

examples.ko: 큰 회사에 대적하려면 좋은 아이디어가 필요해요.
examples.en: To go up against a big company, you need good ideas.

explain: 힘이 비슷하거나 더 센 상대와 맞서 겨룰 때 써요. 보통 '~와/과 대적하다' 꼴이고, '대적할 사람이 없다', '대적할 수 없다'처럼 부정문에서 특히 많이 나와요. 일상에서는 '맞서다'가 더 편하게 들려요.
explain_en: Use it when standing against and competing with an opponent of equal or greater strength. It usually takes the form '~와/과 대적하다', and it appears especially often in negatives such as '대적할 사람이 없다' or '대적할 수 없다'. In daily talk '맞서다' sounds more natural.

en: insult; desecration (of someone's dignity or beliefs)

examples.ko: 그 말은 우리 모두에 대한 모독이에요.
examples.en: Those words are an insult to all of us.
Criticism came out that it was an affront to religion.
That question felt like an insult to me.

examples.ko: 선생님은 학생들 앞에서 모독을 당했다고 느꼈어요.
examples.en: The teacher felt humiliated in front of the students.
The person who made the insulting remark apologized.
That kind of behavior is close to an outrage.

explain: '모욕'은 사람에게 창피를 주는 것이고, '모독'은 존엄, 신념, 죽은 사람, 종교처럼 소중한 것을 더럽히는 무거운 말이에요. '~에 대한 모독'이라고 자주 써요. 가벼운 말다툼에는 어울리지 않아요.
explain_en: '모욕' is shaming a person, while '모독' is a heavy word for defiling something precious, such as dignity, beliefs, the dead, or religion. It is often used as '~에 대한 모독'. It doesn't suit a light quarrel.

examples.en: Please don't insult the teacher with such words.
He was accused of desecrating the flag.

examples.ko: 죽은 사람을 모독하는 글은 올리면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You must not post writing that defiles the dead.

examples.ko: 그 작품은 종교를 모독한다는 이유로 금지됐어요.
examples.en: That work was banned on the grounds that it insults religion.
They are disrespecting our tradition.
Nobody has the right to insult him.

explain: 사람의 명예나 믿음, 소중한 가치를 깎아내릴 때 써요. '모욕하다'보다 훨씬 무겁고 심각한 말이에요. 목적어로 선생님, 종교, 국기, 죽은 사람처럼 존중받아야 하는 대상이 많이 와요.
explain_en: Use it for tearing down someone's honor, faith, or cherished values. It is much heavier and more serious than '모욕하다'. Its objects are often things that should be respected, such as a teacher, a religion, a flag, or the dead.
